config.motion: This house would ban smartphones in schools

points: A blanket ban punishes kids using phones as a lifeline.
It ignores the real driver: how devices are designed.
It dodges digital literacy and regulating companies.
Phone-free lessons with medical exceptions fit the evidence.
A ban is compulsion, and compulsion demands a burden met.
A blanket prohibition punishes the disciplined many for the distracted few.
Narrower tools already exist: device policies, locked pouches, teacher discretion.
Prohibition cedes teaching judgment for commanding obedience.
Schools aren't a treatment; effects vary by age band, so estimate a range.
Bans push use into transit and homes unless parents are brought in.
Credible evidence on learning is thin and mostly correlational.
A graded ban on lessons survives the evidence; a blanket ban doesn't.

verdict.keyDisagreement: Whether the motion's full ban is warranted when the evidence only supports phone-free lessons with narrow exceptions.
verdict.rationale: The debate turned on the gap between what the motion commands and what the panelists agreed the evidence could carry. Amara, Victor and Mei each argued from that gap toward narrower tools, while the prohibitionist case for a full ban was not defended in the turns shown.
